Experts share best practices for considering water filters – whether you’re drinking municipally treated water or relying on a well Adrienne Matei Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Americans have a lot of questions about their drinking water. How is it treated? What’s in it? Most importantly, is it safe? “I’ve even been out to eat where people overhear me talking about my work and come over to ask me a question about their tap water,” said Kimberly Parker, an environmental engineer who studies chemical contaminants in drinking water at Washington University in St Louis. Most Americans have access to municipal water, which “tends to be really well treated” and largely safe to drink, said Parker. Across the US, water is monitored for contamination via centralized infrastructure at federal and state levels. In Parker’s experience, “many environmental engineers choose not to use filtered water” because of their informed confidence in the safety of tap water, she said. Nevertheless, whether you’re drinking municipally treated water or relying on a well, there are water-safety challenges. “There has been a myth in the United States that drinking water is safe for everyone,” said Yolanda McDonald, lead investigator of the Drinking Water Justice Lab at Vanderbilt University. “We know that’s not true.” Her work maps where US drinking water fails to meet federal standards, including Flint , Michigan, and Jackson, Mississippi, where communities have suffered from water sector failures. There’s no one-size-fits-all way to ensure your drinking water is safe. Whether you need to worry about your tap water and what you should do to purify it depends on three things: what’s in your water, where it comes from and your own health. What contaminants most commonly affect US drinking water? Water treatment plants test drinking water for more than 90 contaminants before releasing it into the network of mains and pipes that lead to your tap. But tap water may still contain herbicides and pesticides, industrial pollutants, Pfas and heavy metals. The US Geological Survey estimates 45% of America’s tap water is contaminated with Pfas, and well water is particularly vulnerable to nitrate pollution from agricultural chemicals. One type of pollutant, trihalomethanes (THMs), are actually a byproduct of the tap water treatment process, making them a relatively common issue. In the US, water treatment plants use chlorine to prevent life-threatening waterborne illnesses caused by viruses, bacteria and protozoa in drinking water – cholera is one well-known example. However, the disinfection process creates THMs, which form when the chlorine reacts with organic matter in the water, such as leaf litter, said Parker. While the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) does not consider short-term or low-level exposure to THMs dangerous, when chronically present in drinking water in concentrations over 80 parts per billion (ppb) it’s “possibly carcinogenic”, according to the Massachusetts department of environmental protection . They may also pose risks to the liver, kidneys and reproductive system, though these effects are still being studied. The vast majority of US water utilities are in compliance with the EPA’s Safe Drinking Water Act, said Parker. “When violations do occur, disinfection by-products, including THMs, are one of the most common causes.” We sampled tap water across the US – and found arsenic, lead and toxic chemicals Read more Lead, a neurotoxin, can also be a serious issue, as no level is safe to consume. Under the Biden administration, the EPA estimated 9m lead service lines were still in use in America, though in Trump’s second term that estimate dropped to 4m based on alternate data some watchdogs have questioned . Lead pipes represent a huge infrastructure issue. “Every day throughout the United States, there are communities where our pipes do need to be replaced,” said McDonald. How do I test my drinking water? Start by looking up your city or county’s local Consumer Confidence Report , a water safety document the EPA requires all municipal water systems to produce.
